questions.stem:
(a) Describe any four features of a multiple shop. [8 marks]
(b) Give any four reasons why small scale retailing is common in Nigeria. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
8 marks: (a) four features, 2 marks each: a chain of ten or more branches owned by one firm; uniform shop front, layout and prices; centralised buying and administration at head office; branch managers control each branch; sell standardised/branded goods; located in busy streets of many towns; cash sales mainly
12 marks: (b) four reasons, 3 marks each: small capital required; easy to establish (few legal formalities); low income of consumers who buy in small quantities; personal services and credit to customers; the retailer can locate near consumers; flexible opening hours; lack of skills/education needed for large-scale business; unemployment makes it a source of livelihood
questions.explanation: (a) A multiple shop is one of a chain of branches (usually ten or more) owned by one company. The branches have the same shop front, layout and prices. Buying, advertising and administration are centralised at head office, which supplies the branches. Each branch is run by a manager accountable to head office, and they usually sell standardised goods for cash in busy town centres. (b) Small-scale retailing is common in Nigeria because little capital is needed to start; there are few legal formalities; consumers have low incomes and buy in small quantities; the small retailer gives personal service, credit and convenient hours near consumers' homes; and it provides self-employment for people with limited skills or education.

questions.stem:
(a) State any four sources of capital for a public limited company. [4 marks]
(b) Explain any four advantages and disadvantages respectively of converting a business into a public limited company. [16 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) any four, 1 mark each: issue of shares (ordinary/preference); debentures; bank loans and overdrafts; ploughed-back profits (retained earnings); trade credit; hire purchase/leasing; government grants
8 marks: (b) four advantages, 2 marks each: large capital can be raised from the public; limited liability of shareholders; continuity (perpetual succession); shares freely transferable on the stock exchange; economies of scale; professional management; greater public confidence/credit-worthiness
8 marks: (b) four disadvantages, 2 marks each: costly and complex formation; publication of accounts (loss of secrecy); separation of ownership and control; slow decision making/bureaucracy; heavy taxation; risk of takeover; conflicts between shareholders and management
questions.explanation: (a) Issue of shares, debentures, bank loans and overdrafts, and retained profits (also trade credit and hire purchase). (b) Advantages: large capital can be raised by selling shares to the public; shareholders have limited liability; the company enjoys perpetual succession; shares can be easily transferred on the stock exchange; it can enjoy economies of scale and employ professional managers. Disadvantages: formation is costly with many legal formalities; accounts must be published, so there is no secrecy; ownership is separated from control, so management may not act in shareholders' interest; decisions are slow; and the company faces heavy taxes and possible takeover bids.

questions.stem:
Write short notes on the following, showing their main uses in foreign trade:
(a) Shipping notes; [4 marks]
(b) Ship's manifest; [4 marks]
(c) Bill of sight; [4 marks]
(d) Dock warrant; [4 marks]
(e) Bill of entry. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) shipping note: document sent by the exporter to the port authority/shipping company giving details of goods to be loaded; authorises the goods to be received on board and serves as a receipt from the port (mate's receipt follows)
4 marks: (b) ship's manifest: a list of all the cargo carried on a ship (consignors, consignees, marks, quantities); used by customs to check the cargo landed/loaded and by the port authority
4 marks: (c) bill of sight: a temporary declaration made to customs by an importer who cannot fully describe the goods; allows the goods to be examined/landed before a proper bill of entry is completed
4 marks: (d) dock warrant: a document issued by a dock/warehouse company acknowledging receipt of goods stored; it is a document of title, so ownership of the goods can be transferred by endorsing it
4 marks: (e) bill of entry: a detailed declaration of imported (or exported) goods made to customs, showing their nature, quantity, value and origin; used to assess and pay customs duty and to clear goods
questions.explanation: (a) A shipping note is completed by the exporter and sent to the port or shipping company with the goods, giving their details so that they can be received and loaded. (b) A ship's manifest lists all the cargo on board the ship and is presented to customs at the port of loading and of discharge to check the cargo. (c) A bill of sight is a provisional declaration to customs by an importer who lacks full details of the goods; it lets him inspect the goods before making a full bill of entry. (d) A dock warrant is a receipt issued by a dock warehouse for goods stored there; it is a document of title, so the goods can be sold by endorsing it. (e) A bill of entry is the importer's or exporter's detailed declaration to customs of the goods, used to calculate and pay customs duties and to obtain release of the goods.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the functions of the Stock Exchange. [15 marks]
(b) State the types of securities traded in the Stock Exchange. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
15 marks: (a) any five functions described, 3 marks each: market for buying and selling existing securities (secondary market); helps companies and government raise long-term capital; provides liquidity to investors; values/prices securities and indicates the state of the economy; encourages savings and investment; protects investors by regulating dealers and listed companies; facilitates mergers/acquisitions; mobilises funds for development
5 marks: (b) any five, 1 mark each: ordinary shares; preference shares; debentures; government stocks/bonds (gilt-edged securities); industrial loans/bonds; state/local government bonds; convertible loans
questions.explanation: (a) The stock exchange is a market where existing shares and stocks are bought and sold, which gives investors liquidity because they can easily turn their securities into cash. By assuring investors of this liquidity, it makes it easier for companies and government to raise long-term capital. It fixes the prices of securities, and these act as a barometer of the economy. It encourages savings and investment and directs funds into productive uses. It protects investors through rules for listing and the conduct of dealers. It also aids mergers and takeovers. (b) Ordinary shares, preference shares, debentures, government stocks and bonds (gilt-edged securities), and industrial or state bonds.

15 marks: (b) five services, 3 marks each: encourage regular savings; grant loans to members at low interest; rotating lump-sum contributions (esusu/ajo); safe keeping of members' money; provide guarantees/surety for members; financial advice/education; welfare support in emergencies; bulk purchase of goods for members
questions.explanation: (a) Thrift societies are voluntary associations of people with a common bond, such as workers in one place or members of a community. Members make regular contributions to a common fund, from which they can take loans or collect lump sums in turn (for example esusu or credit and thrift co-operatives). (b) They encourage members to save regularly; they give loans to members at low interest without collateral; members receive rotating lump sums to start or expand businesses; they keep members' savings safely; they stand as guarantors for members seeking other credit; and they give financial advice and welfare support.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five problems of using rail transport in Nigeria. [12 marks]
(b) Write short notes on:
(i) Tramp liners; [4 marks]
(ii) Ocean liners. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) first problem explained, e.g. poor maintenance of tracks, coaches and locomotives leading to breakdowns and accidents
3 marks: (a) second problem explained, e.g. limited network that does not reach many towns
2 marks: (a) third problem, e.g. slowness and frequent delays
2 marks: (a) fourth problem, e.g. inflexibility: fixed routes and timetables, no door-to-door service
2 marks: (a) fifth problem, e.g. obsolete narrow-gauge equipment; poor management, corruption and theft of goods; high cost of expansion
4 marks: (b)(i) tramp ships: cargo ships with no fixed routes or timetables, hired (chartered) to carry bulky cargo wherever there is demand; charges negotiable
4 marks: (b)(ii) ocean liners: ships that sail on regular fixed routes and timetables, carrying passengers and general cargo at fixed rates (conference rates)
questions.explanation: (a) Rail transport in Nigeria suffers from poorly maintained tracks, coaches and locomotives, causing breakdowns and accidents. Its network is limited and does not reach many towns. It is slow, with frequent delays. It is inflexible, running on fixed routes and timetables with no door-to-door service. Its old narrow-gauge equipment limits speed and capacity. Poor management, corruption and theft of goods also discourage users. (b)(i) Tramp ships have no fixed routes or timetables; they are chartered to carry bulky cargo such as grain, coal or timber to any port where there is demand, at negotiated rates. (ii) Ocean liners sail on fixed routes to a regular timetable, carrying passengers and mixed cargo at published rates whether or not they are full.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a contract of sale of goods? [5 marks]
(b) State any three of its provisions. [9 marks]
(c) Explain two conditions that constitute acceptance in the contract of sale of goods. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) a contract by which the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the ownership (property) in goods to the buyer for a money consideration called the price
9 marks: (b) any three implied terms/provisions, 3 marks each: the seller has the right (title) to sell; goods must correspond with their description; goods must be of merchantable quality; goods must be fit for the purpose made known; in a sale by sample, bulk must correspond with the sample; rules on passing of property and risk
6 marks: (c) two conditions, 3 marks each: the buyer intimates to the seller that he has accepted the goods; the buyer does an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership (e.g. uses/resells the goods); the buyer retains the goods beyond a reasonable time without rejecting them
questions.explanation: (a) A contract of sale of goods is one in which the seller transfers, or agrees to transfer, ownership of goods to the buyer in return for money called the price. (b) Under the Sale of Goods Act the seller must have the right to sell the goods; the goods must correspond with their description; they must be of merchantable quality; they must be fit for the purpose the buyer made known; and in a sale by sample the bulk must correspond with the sample. (c) The buyer is deemed to have accepted the goods when he tells the seller he has accepted them; when he does something inconsistent with the seller's ownership, such as reselling or using them; or when he keeps them beyond a reasonable time without rejecting them.

questions.explanation: (a) Public relations is the deliberate, planned and sustained effort to create and maintain goodwill and mutual understanding between an organisation and its publics: customers, employees, government and the community. (b) A firm can issue press releases and hold press conferences; sponsor sports, cultural and educational events; donate to charities and community projects such as roads and boreholes; hold open days, factory tours and trade exhibitions; publish house journals and newsletters; award scholarships; and give courteous customer service and after-sales service.

questions.stem: Mention and explain any four environments under which a business operates.
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: Economic environment: income levels, inflation, interest and exchange rates, taxation and competition that affect demand and costs
5 marks: Political/legal environment: government policies, laws and regulations, stability of government affecting business operations
5 marks: Social/cultural environment: population, customs, beliefs, tastes, education and lifestyle of the people
5 marks: Technological environment: level of technology, machinery and innovation (also accept physical/natural environment: climate, location, natural resources; or competitive environment)
questions.explanation: The economic environment covers income levels, inflation, interest rates, exchange rates, taxes and competition, which affect demand and costs. The political and legal environment covers government policies, laws, regulations and political stability, which determine what a business may do and how secure it is. The social and cultural environment covers the size and structure of the population and its customs, religion, tastes and education, which affect what goods are demanded. The technological environment covers the state of technology and innovation, which affects production methods, costs and products. The physical environment (climate, natural resources, location) is also acceptable.

questions.stem:

(c) What are the objectives of the Lake Chad Basin Commission? [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) any five, 1 mark each: Chamber of Commerce (e.g. Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry); Manufacturers Association of Nigeria; Nigeria Employers' Consultative Association; Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (NACCIMA); market women associations; National Association of Road Transport Owners; Association of Nigerian Bakers
6 marks: (b) three functions, 2 marks each: negotiate with trade unions on wages and conditions of service; represent employers before government; advise members on labour laws/industrial relations; promote good industrial relations and settle disputes; research and training
9 marks: (c) three objectives, 3 marks each: to regulate and control the use of the water and other resources of the Lake Chad basin; to promote regional co-operation and integrated development among member states (Nigeria, Niger, Chad, Cameroon); to plan and co-ordinate development projects such as irrigation, fishing, agriculture and livestock; to settle disputes and protect the environment of the basin
questions.explanation: (a) Chambers of Commerce, the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN), the Nigeria Employers' Consultative Association (NECA), NACCIMA, and market traders' and transport owners' associations. (b) An employers' association negotiates wages and conditions of service with trade unions on behalf of employers; it represents employers' views to government; and it advises members on labour laws and helps settle industrial disputes. (c) The Lake Chad Basin Commission (Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon, later others) aims to regulate and control the use of the basin's water and other natural resources; to promote co-operation and joint development projects in agriculture, irrigation, fishing and livestock among member states; and to protect the basin environment and settle disputes among members.

Explain each of the following documents:
(i) Export invoice [4 marks]
(ii) Bill of lading [4 marks]
(iii) Certificate of Origin [4 marks]
(iv) Bill of exchange [4 marks]
(v) Consular invoice [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (i) export invoice: a bill sent by the exporter to the overseas buyer stating the goods sent, their quantity, price, terms of sale and total amount payable
4 marks: (ii) bill of lading: issued by the shipping company; a receipt for goods shipped, evidence of the contract of carriage, and a document of title that must be produced to collect the goods
4 marks: (iii) certificate of origin: a document, usually issued by a chamber of commerce, stating the country where the goods were made; used to determine duty/preferential tariffs and enforce trade restrictions
4 marks: (iv) bill of exchange: an unconditional order in writing addressed by one person (drawer) to another (drawee), signed by the drawer, requiring the drawee to pay on demand or at a fixed future time a sum certain in money to a specified person or bearer; used to settle international payments
4 marks: (v) consular invoice: an invoice certified by the consul of the importing country in the exporting country, confirming that the prices and details are correct; prevents dumping/under-invoicing and helps customs assess duty
questions.explanation: (i) An export invoice is the exporter's bill to the foreign buyer, showing the goods, quantity, price, terms and amount due. (ii) A bill of lading is issued by the shipping company. It is a receipt for the goods shipped, evidence of the contract of carriage and a document of title; the importer must present it to collect the goods. (iii) A certificate of origin states the country where the goods were produced; customs use it to apply the correct or preferential duties. (iv) A bill of exchange is an unconditional written order from a drawer to a drawee to pay a certain sum on demand or at a fixed future date to a named person or bearer; it is widely used to settle foreign trade debts. (v) A consular invoice is certified by the importing country's consul in the exporting country, confirming the price and details, to prevent dumping and to help assess duty.

questions.stem: State and explain five functions of commerce.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: Removes the hindrance of persons/ownership: trade links producers and consumers (buying and selling)
4 marks: Removes the hindrance of place: transport moves goods from where they are produced to where they are needed
4 marks: Removes the hindrance of time: warehousing stores goods until they are needed
4 marks: Removes the hindrance of risk: insurance covers business risks; and of finance: banking provides capital and means of payment
4 marks: Removes the hindrance of knowledge/information: advertising and communication inform consumers about goods; also raises standard of living and promotes international relations
questions.explanation: Commerce removes the hindrances that stand between production and consumption. Trade (buying and selling) brings producers and consumers together and removes the hindrance of persons. Transport moves goods to where they are needed, removing the hindrance of place. Warehousing stores goods until they are needed, removing the hindrance of time. Insurance protects traders against loss, removing the hindrance of risk. Banking provides finance and convenient means of payment. Advertising and communication inform consumers, removing the hindrance of knowledge. Together these raise living standards and promote trade between nations.

questions.explanation: (a) The principal must pay the agent's agreed commission; reimburse expenses the agent properly incurs; indemnify the agent against losses and liabilities arising from lawful performance of his duties; provide the information and documents the agent needs; and not obstruct the agent. (b) A valid contract requires: an offer, a definite proposal by one party; acceptance, unconditional agreement to the terms of the offer; consideration, something of value given by each side; capacity, meaning the parties are legally able to contract (e.g. not minors or insane persons); and an intention to create legal relations, with a lawful object and genuine consent.

It is also used where middlemen are unreliable or the producer can afford his own outlets. (b) A manufacturer brands products to distinguish them from competitors'; to make advertising easier; to build customer loyalty and repeat sales; to guarantee consistent quality and price; and to protect the product legally against imitation.

questions.stem:
A large-scale retail concern had the following balances in its books as at 31st December, 1998:
Stock 1st January, 1998 N8,000; Purchases during the year N85,000; Sales for the year N120,000; Stock 31st December, 1998 N7,000; Selling expenses N10,000.
(a) You are required to calculate:
(i) Cost of goods sold; [5 marks]
(ii) Net profit; [7 marks]
(iii) Rate of stock turnover [3 marks]
(b) State five factors that may lead to an increase in the rate of stock turnover of a business. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a)(i) cost of goods sold = 8,000 + 85,000 - 7,000 = N86,000
4 marks: (a)(ii) gross profit = 120,000 - 86,000 = N34,000
3 marks: (a)(ii) net profit = 34,000 - selling expenses 10,000 = N24,000
3 marks: (a)(iii) average stock (8,000 + 7,000)/2 = 7,500; rate of stock turnover = 86,000 / 7,500 = 11.47 times (about 11 times)
5 marks: (b) any five, 1 mark each: reduction in selling price; effective advertising and sales promotion; increased demand/rising incomes; good quality goods; good location; granting credit facilities; good customer service; keeping low stock levels; selling fast-moving/fashionable goods
questions.explanation: (a)(i) Cost of goods sold = opening stock 8,000 + purchases 85,000 - closing stock 7,000 = N86,000. (ii) Gross profit = 120,000 - 86,000 = 34,000. Net profit = 34,000 - 10,000 = N24,000. (iii) Average stock = (8,000 + 7,000) / 2 = 7,500; rate of stock turnover = 86,000 / 7,500 = 11.47 times a year. (b) It may rise because of lower selling prices, effective advertising and sales promotion, higher consumer incomes and demand, good quality and fashionable goods, a good location, credit facilities to customers, or good customer service.

Corruption and mismanagement are common. They often make losses that burden the government budget, and lack of competition leads to poor services.

2 marks: (a) capital: man-made goods used to produce other goods (machines, tools, buildings); reward is interest

The entrepreneur organises the other factors and bears the risks of production; his reward is profit. (b) Land is a free gift of nature, fixed in supply and immobile. Labour cannot be separated from the worker, cannot be stored, and is mobile. Capital is man-made, depreciates with use and depends on savings. questions.explanation: (a) Money is a medium of exchange: it is generally accepted in payment, which removes the double coincidence of wants of barter. It is a unit of account (measure of value): the prices of goods are expressed in money, making comparison easy. It is a store of value: wealth can be kept in money for future use. It is a standard of deferred payment: debts and future payments are expressed in money. (b)(i) Current accounts allow withdrawals at any time by cheque, earn little or no interest, attract bank charges, and may be given overdrafts. (ii) Fixed deposits are kept for a fixed period, earn a higher interest rate, need notice before withdrawal, and have no cheque book.

questions.explanation: (a) A contract is an agreement between two or more parties that is enforceable by law. (b) It may be ended by performance, when both parties fulfil their obligations; by agreement, when both decide to end it or replace it with a new one; by breach, when one party fails to perform, so the other may treat it as ended and sue for damages; and by frustration, when an event beyond their control (such as destruction of the goods) makes performance impossible. (a) consular invoice; [4 marks]
(b) indent; [4 marks]
(c) bill of lading; [4 marks]
(d) certificate of origin; [4 marks]
(e) certificate of insurance. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) consular invoice: an invoice certified by the consul of the importing country in the exporting country confirming the price/details, used to prevent under-invoicing/dumping and assess duty
4 marks: (b) indent: an order placed by an importer through an indent (export commission) agent for goods from abroad; may be open (no supplier named) or closed/specific (supplier named)
4 marks: (c) bill of lading: issued by the shipping company; receipt for goods shipped, evidence of contract of carriage and document of title
4 marks: (d) certificate of origin: states the country of manufacture of the goods; used to determine duties/preferential tariffs
4 marks: (e) certificate of insurance: evidence that the goods are insured against risks during the voyage, showing the value insured and risks covered; used to claim compensation
questions.explanation: (a) A consular invoice is certified by the consul of the importing country in the exporting country to confirm the value and details of the goods; it prevents dumping and helps customs assess duty. (b) An indent is an order for foreign goods placed by an importer through an indent (export commission) agent. It is open if any supplier may be used, and closed if a particular supplier is named. (c) A bill of lading is issued by the shipping company; it is a receipt for the goods, evidence of the contract of carriage and a document of title. (d) A certificate of origin states the country where the goods were made, so the correct or preferential duty can be charged. (e) A certificate of insurance proves that the goods are insured for the voyage, stating the value and risks covered, and is used to claim compensation if they are lost or damaged.

(d) gross profit percentage (%); [3 marks]

3 marks: (b) net profit = 60,000 - wages and salaries 15,000 = N45,000
3 marks: (c) average stock = (15,000 + 20,000) / 2 = N17,500
3 marks: (c) rate of turnover = 60,000 / 17,500 = 3.43 times
3 marks: (d) gross profit percentage = 60,000 / 120,000 x 100 = 50%

questions.explanation: (a) Cost of goods sold = opening stock 15,000 + purchases 65,000 - closing stock 20,000 = 60,000; gross profit = 120,000 - 60,000 = N60,000. (b) Net profit = 60,000 - 15,000 = N45,000 (debtors are an asset, not an expense). (c) Average stock = (15,000 + 20,000) / 2 = 17,500; rate of turnover = 60,000 / 17,500 = 3.43 times. questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) ordinary shares (equity): shares whose holders own the company, have voting rights, receive a variable dividend after preference shareholders, and bear the greatest risk
4 marks: (b) preference shares: shares that receive a fixed rate of dividend before ordinary shares and are repaid first on liquidation; usually no voting rights
4 marks: (c) stags: speculators who apply for new issues of shares hoping to sell them at a premium as soon as dealing starts
4 marks: (d) bulls: speculators who buy shares expecting prices to rise so as to sell later at a profit
4 marks: (e) stockbrokers: agents who buy and sell securities on behalf of clients for a commission and advise investors
questions.explanation: (a) Ordinary shares carry ownership and voting rights; holders receive a variable dividend after preference shareholders and bear the highest risk. (b) Preference shares carry a fixed dividend paid before ordinary dividends and are repaid first on winding up, but usually have no voting rights. (c) Stags apply for new shares hoping to sell them quickly at a premium when trading begins. (d) Bulls buy shares expecting prices to rise, so they can sell later at a profit. (e) Stockbrokers are agents who buy and sell securities for clients on the stock exchange in return for commission, and advise investors.

questions.explanation: (a) An occupation is any lawful activity that a person engages in regularly to earn a living. (b) Occupation has three branches. Industrial occupations are extractive (mining, fishing, farming), manufacturing (baking, textile making) and constructive (building, road construction). Commercial occupations are trade, which is home trade (retail and wholesale) or foreign trade (import, export, entrepot), and aids to trade (transport, banking, insurance, warehousing, communication, advertising). Services are direct (doctors, teachers, lawyers) or indirect (police, soldiers, civil servants). The diagram is a tree with Occupation at the top branching into Industrial, Commercial and Services, each branching further as above.

questions.explanation: (a) Bonded warehouses, public warehouses, private (manufacturers') warehouses, wholesalers' warehouses, and cold storage warehouses. (b) Warehousing allows goods to be produced ahead of demand and stored until needed, creating time utility. It stabilises prices because stored goods are released when supply is short. It protects goods from damage, deterioration and theft. It ensures a regular supply of seasonal goods throughout the year. It allows goods to be graded, packed and blended before sale. In a bonded warehouse importers can pay duty only when goods are withdrawn, and dock warrants issued on stored goods can be used as security for loans.

Goods are attractively displayed to encourage impulse buying, a wide variety is stocked, and sales are mainly for cash.

(b) Advantages: large capital can be raised from the public; members have limited liability; the company has perpetual succession; shares are freely transferable on the stock exchange; it can enjoy economies of scale and hire specialists. 4 marks: Debentures: long-term loans to a company at a fixed rate of interest; holders are creditors, not owners; may be secured on assets

4 marks: Any other one: stocks (consolidated fully paid shares); state/local government bonds; industrial loans; convertible loan stock
questions.explanation: Ordinary shares give their holders ownership and voting rights, with a variable dividend paid after preference shareholders; they carry the highest risk. Preference shares earn a fixed dividend paid before ordinary dividends and are repaid first on winding up; they may be cumulative, participating or redeemable. Debentures are long-term loans to a company at a fixed rate of interest; holders are creditors and may be secured on the company's assets. Government stocks or bonds (gilt-edged securities) are loans to government at fixed interest and are very safe. Stocks are fully paid shares consolidated into units that can be traded in any amount; state government bonds and convertible loans are also traded.

(v) Bearer cheque. [2 marks]
(b) Explain five means of payment in business. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) stale cheque: a cheque presented after a long period (usually six months) from its date, which the bank will not pay
2 marks: (a)(ii) post-dated cheque: a cheque bearing a future date; cannot be paid before that date
2 marks: (a)(iii) dishonoured cheque: a cheque the bank refuses to pay, e.g. for insufficient funds, irregular signature or alterations, marked 'refer to drawer'
2 marks: (a)(iv) crossed cheque: a cheque with two parallel lines across its face; it cannot be cashed over the counter and must be paid into a bank account
2 marks: (a)(v) bearer cheque: a cheque payable to whoever presents it (the bearer); can be cashed over the counter without endorsement
10 marks: (b) five means explained, 2 marks each: cash (coins and notes, legal tender); cheque; bank draft; standing order/direct debit; credit transfer; postal and money orders; credit/debit cards and electronic transfers (ATM, POS, internet banking); bill of exchange; letter of credit
questions.explanation: (a)(i) A stale cheque is one presented long after its date (usually more than six months), so the bank will not pay it. (ii) A post-dated cheque carries a future date and cannot be paid before that date. (iii) A dishonoured cheque is one the bank refuses to pay, for example because of insufficient funds or an irregular signature. (iv) A crossed cheque has two parallel lines across it and must be paid into a bank account, not cashed over the counter. (v) A bearer cheque is payable to whoever presents it. (b) Cash (coins and notes) is legal tender for immediate payment. A cheque is a written order to a bank to pay a stated sum. A bank draft is a cheque drawn by a bank on itself and is safe for large payments. A standing order is an instruction to the bank to pay regular fixed sums. Electronic payments by debit or credit card, ATM, POS and internet transfer allow instant settlement. Postal orders and money orders are post office means of remitting money.

questions.markingGuide:

questions.explanation: (a) In a credit sale ownership passes to the buyer at once and, if he defaults, the seller can only sue for the balance. In hire purchase ownership passes only when the last instalment is paid, and the seller may repossess the goods on default. (b) Broker, factor, del credere agent, auctioneer and commission agent. (c) A broker brings buyers and sellers together and negotiates terms without holding the goods. A factor takes possession of goods and sells them in his own name, collecting payment. A del credere agent sells on behalf of the principal and guarantees that buyers will pay. An auctioneer sells goods publicly to the highest bidder and collects the price. A commission agent buys or sells for a principal in return for commission and arranges delivery.

questions.stem:
Madam Ajaratu is a retailer. On 1st March, 2010, she bought goods costing Le510,000 and paid Le40,000 to bring the goods to her shop. She sold the goods on 3rd March, 2010 to Mr. Adamu at a catalogue price of Le800,000 subject to 20% trade discount.
To encourage Mr. Adamu to pay before the end of March, Madam Ajaratu gave him 5% cash discount. Mr. Adamu paid Madam Ajaratu on March 18, 2010.
Required:
(a) State two uses of trade discount. [4 marks]
(b) Calculate the selling price of the goods sold to Mr. Adamu. [4 marks]
(c) How much did Adamu pay to Madam Ajaratu on March 18, 2010? [4 marks]
(d) Calculate Madam Ajaratu's:
(i) gross profit; [4 marks]
(ii) gross profit percentage. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) two uses, 2 marks each: to give the retailer a margin of profit when selling at the catalogue price; to encourage bulk buying; to attract/retain trade customers; to conceal the actual price from final consumers
4 marks: (b) selling price = 800,000 - 20% (160,000) = Le640,000
4 marks: (c) cash discount 5% of 640,000 = 32,000; amount paid = Le608,000
4 marks: (d)(i) cost of goods = 510,000 + carriage 40,000 = 550,000; gross profit = 640,000 - 550,000 = Le90,000
4 marks: (d)(ii) gross profit percentage = 90,000 / 640,000 x 100 = 14.06% (on sales)
questions.explanation: (a) Trade discount gives the retailer a margin of profit when goods are resold at the catalogue price, and it encourages bulk buying by trade customers. (b) Selling price = 800,000 - 20% of 800,000 (160,000) = Le640,000. (c) Cash discount = 5% of 640,000 = 32,000, so Adamu paid 640,000 - 32,000 = Le608,000. (d)(i) Cost of goods = 510,000 + carriage inwards 40,000 = 550,000; gross profit = 640,000 - 550,000 = Le90,000. The cash discount is a finance expense charged against net profit, not gross profit. (ii) Gross profit percentage on sales = 90,000 / 640,000 x 100 = 14.06%.
